entries.title: The Sun
entries.summary: Our star: a ball of hot plasma about 109 times wider than Earth, shining by nuclear fusion in its core for roughly 4.6 billion years.
body: The Sun is a G-type main-sequence star (spectral type G2 V). It has about 333,000 times the mass of Earth, far more than all the planets together.

Its mass is known through gravity. The orbits of planets and spacecraft measure the product **GM** (gravitational constant times mass) very precisely; dividing by the constant G, which is known far less precisely, gives the mass in kilograms.

The Sun has no solid surface. What we see is the photosphere, with an effective temperature of 5,772 K. Conditions deep inside, such as a central temperature near 15.7 million K, come from solar models rather than direct measurement.
The Sun does not rotate like a solid ball: its equator spins faster than its poles. The adopted period of about 25.4 days applies at 16 degrees latitude.
The age of the Solar System, about 4.567 billion years, comes from radioactive dating of the oldest grains in meteorites. The Sun is assumed to have formed at almost the same time.
In the game the Sun's size, position and brightness use measured values, but its glowing look is **Generated** from its temperature. It is not an image of the real Sun.

entries.title: Mercury
entries.summary: The smallest planet and the closest to the Sun: an airless, cratered world that spins three times for every two trips around the Sun.
body: Mercury is only about 38% of Earth's width, yet it is dense, with a mean density close to Earth's. Its orbit takes 88 Earth days and is the most elongated of the eight planets in this game (eccentricity 0.21).
It rotates once every 58.6 days, exactly two thirds of its year. Combined with its orbital motion, this makes one solar day (sunrise to sunrise) last about 176 Earth days, two full Mercury years.
Mercury has no real atmosphere, only a thin exosphere that is essentially a vacuum. Its average temperature is about 440 K, reaching 590-725 K on the side facing the Sun.
Even so, radar-bright deposits near its north pole are water ice. NASA's MESSENGER spacecraft confirmed this with its neutron spectrometer in 2012.

In the game, Mercury's colours come from a Solar System Scope map based on spacecraft imagery. The hills and craters you fly over at low altitude are **Generated** detail, not Mercury's real topography.

entries.title: Venus
entries.summary: Earth's near-twin in size, wrapped in a crushing carbon-dioxide atmosphere that makes it the hottest planet in the Solar System.
body: Venus is 95% of Earth's diameter and 81% of its mass, but its surface is hostile: the average temperature is about 737 K (464 °C) and the surface pressure is about 90 times Earth's.
Its atmosphere is 96.5% carbon dioxide. That thick blanket traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect, which is why Venus is hotter than Mercury even though it is almost twice as far from the Sun.
Venus spins backwards compared with most planets, and very slowly: one rotation takes 243 Earth days, longer than its 225-day year. A solar day on Venus lasts about 117 Earth days.
Dense, persistent clouds of corrosive acid hide the surface from view in visible light. Underneath, the surface has volcanoes and deformed mountains.
In the game, Venus is drawn as its cloud tops using an artist-processed map, and its haze is a **Generated** approximation chosen to look plausible. Neither is a photograph.

entries.title: Earth
entries.summary: Our home planet: the only world known to host life, with liquid-water oceans, a nitrogen-oxygen atmosphere and a magnetic field.
body: Earth is slightly flattened by its rotation: its equatorial radius is about 21 km larger than its polar radius. It orbits the Sun once every 365.256 days and spins once every 23.93 hours relative to the stars.
Dry air is 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, with argon, carbon dioxide and traces of other gases. The carbon dioxide level, about 420 parts per million on the fact sheet, is rising and changes with time.
Earth is the only place we know of that is inhabited by living things. Whether life exists anywhere else is an open question.

In the game, Earth's colours come from NASA's Blue Marble Next Generation map for July 2004, its night lights from NASA's Black Marble 2016, and its clouds from a fixed 2002 snapshot, not today's weather. Mountains and ocean coasts follow NOAA's ETOPO 2022 elevation data at about 7 km spacing; anything finer is **Generated** detail.
The blue sky and red sunsets you see are computed with a published scattering model using measured properties of air, so the colours are **Inferred**, not painted.

entries.title: The Moon
entries.summary: Earth's only natural satellite: a cratered, airless world that always turns the same face towards us and is slowly drifting away.
body: The Moon is about a quarter of Earth's width. It orbits Earth every 27.3 days and rotates exactly once per orbit, so the same hemisphere always faces Earth. This is called tidal locking.

It is moving away from Earth by about 3.8 cm per year, while tides slowly lengthen Earth's day. Lunar laser ranging, one of the data sets behind JPL's ephemerides, tracks the Moon's distance precisely.
Most scientists think the Moon formed from debris thrown out when a large body struck the young Earth. This giant-impact idea is a well-supported model, not something anyone observed.
With almost no atmosphere, the surface swings from about 95 K at night to 390 K by day at the equator. Apollo astronauts brought back 382 kg of lunar rock and soil.

In the game, the Moon's colours come from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera mosaic (via NASA's CGI Moon Kit) and its mountains and craters from the LRO laser altimeter (LOLA). Near the poles the colour map is filled from a lower-resolution altimeter brightness map. Detail smaller than a few kilometres is **Generated**.

entries.title: Mars
entries.summary: The cold, dusty red planet: a desert world with a thin carbon-dioxide atmosphere and clear evidence that liquid water once pooled on its surface.
body: Mars is about half Earth's width, with a day only 40 minutes longer than ours and a tilt similar to Earth's, so it has seasons. Its year lasts 687 Earth days.
The atmosphere is thin, mostly carbon dioxide, with an average surface pressure of about 6 millibars, less than 1% of Earth's. The average temperature is around 214 K (-59 °C).
Rocks studied by the Curiosity rover in Gale crater show that an ancient lake once existed there, with water that could have supported microbial life. No life has been found on Mars.
Fine dust in the Martian air scatters light differently from Earth's air: Curiosity photographed sunsets that look bluish around the Sun.

In the game, Mars's colours come from a Solar System Scope map, and its haze is a **Generated** artistic approximation. The relief you fly over is **Generated** too: the game does not yet use Mars's real laser-altimeter topography.

entries.title: Phobos
entries.summary: The larger of Mars's two small, lumpy moons, orbiting so close that it circles the planet three times a day and is slowly spiralling inward.
body: Phobos is not round: it measures about 26 by 23 by 18 km. Asaph Hall discovered it, together with Deimos, in 1877.
It orbits only about 6,000 km above Mars's surface, completing an orbit in 7.65 hours, faster than Mars rotates.
Tides are pulling Phobos closer to Mars by about 1.8 m per century. NASA expects it to crash into Mars or break up into a ring in roughly 50 million years; this is a prediction, not an observation.
Both Martian moons look like dark, carbon-rich asteroids, but their origin is still debated: they may be captured asteroids, though some evidence contradicts that idea.
In the game, Phobos's map comes from spacecraft images collected in NASA's 3D Resources; small-scale relief is **Generated**.

entries.title: Deimos
entries.summary: Mars's smaller, outer moon: a dark, irregular body only about 12 km across, with craters partly filled by loose material.
body: Deimos measures roughly 16 by 12 by 10 km and orbits Mars every 30.3 hours at about 23,500 km from the planet's centre.
Like Phobos, it looks like a dark, carbon-rich asteroid of the kind found in the outer asteroid belt. Its craters are partly filled in, which gives it a smoother look than Phobos.
Its mean density, about 1.5 g/cm³ with an uncertainty of about 11%, is derived from its measured gravitational pull and its size.
Asaph Hall discovered Deimos in 1877, the same year he found Phobos.
In the game, Deimos's map comes from spacecraft images collected in NASA's 3D Resources; small-scale relief is **Generated**.

entries.title: Jupiter
entries.summary: The largest planet: a giant ball of hydrogen and helium with no solid surface, banded clouds and a storm wider than Earth.
body: Jupiter has about 318 times Earth's mass, roughly two and a half times the mass of all the other planets combined. It spins in under 10 hours, which flattens it visibly at the poles.
It has no solid surface. Its atmosphere is about 90% hydrogen and 10% helium, and the pressure keeps rising with depth to far beyond 1,000 bars.
The Great Red Spot is a storm bigger than Earth that, according to NASA, has raged for hundreds of years.

NASA's Juno spacecraft, which began its science orbits of Jupiter in 2016, measured Jupiter's gravity field about ten times more precisely than before and saw weather features reaching below the 100-bar level. Its results bear on whether Jupiter has a core, and how big it is.
In the game, Jupiter's clouds come from a Solar System Scope map based on spacecraft imagery. Real clouds change from month to month, so this is a fixed snapshot. Its thin limb haze is **Generated**.

entries.title: Io
entries.summary: The innermost of Jupiter's four large moons and, according to NASA, the most volcanically active world in the Solar System, heated from inside by tides.
body: Io is slightly larger than Earth's Moon. Galileo Galilei discovered it in 1610, together with Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.
In 1979 an image taken by Voyager for navigation showed volcanic plumes rising from Io: the first evidence of active volcanism on any world other than Earth.

Around the time of Voyager 1's flyby, Peale, Cassen and Reynolds predicted that energy released by tidal flexing could melt much of Io's interior, and that the effects might be visible in Voyager's pictures.
Io's orbital period is almost exactly half of Europa's and a quarter of Ganymede's. This rhythm, a resonance, keeps the moons tugging on each other again and again.
In the game, Io's map comes from spacecraft images collected in NASA's 3D Resources; volcanic relief at small scales is **Generated**.

entries.title: Europa
entries.summary: A bright, icy moon of Jupiter, slightly smaller than our Moon, with strong evidence for a salty ocean hidden beneath its frozen crust.
body: Europa is a little smaller than Earth's Moon and covered by bright ice. It orbits Jupiter every 3.55 days, always keeping the same face towards the planet.

As Jupiter's tilted magnetic field sweeps past, Europa responds with a changing magnetic field of its own. NASA's Galileo spacecraft measured this, and the simplest explanation is an electric current flowing in a global layer of salty liquid water beneath the ice.
That ocean is **Inferred**: no one has seen or sampled it. Its depth and saltiness are not yet known.
NASA's Europa Clipper launched on 14 October 2024 and is due at Jupiter in April 2030, where it plans 49 close flybys of Europa. ESA's Juice mission will also observe it.
In the game, Europa's map comes from spacecraft images collected in NASA's 3D Resources; fine relief is **Generated**.

entries.title: Ganymede
entries.summary: The largest moon in the Solar System, bigger than the planet Mercury, and the only moon known to generate its own magnetic field.
body: Ganymede is wider than Mercury, though it has less than half of Mercury's mass. Its low density, about 1.94 g/cm³, fits a mixture of rock and ice, and NASA describes layers of rock and ice around a core.

In 1996 NASA's Galileo spacecraft discovered that Ganymede has its own internal magnetic field, about 750 nanotesla at the equator. It is the only moon known to have one, and it produces auroras around the moon's poles.

The Hubble Space Telescope watched those auroral ovals rock back and forth as Jupiter's field changes. They rock less than expected for a solid moon, which points to a salty, electrically conducting ocean deep beneath the ice. The ocean is **Inferred**, not seen.
ESA's Juice spacecraft, launched on 14 April 2023, is due at Jupiter in July 2031 and will make Ganymede its primary target.
In the game, Ganymede's map comes from spacecraft images collected in NASA's 3D Resources; fine relief is **Generated**.

entries.title: Callisto
entries.summary: Jupiter's outermost large moon: a dark world that NASA calls the most heavily cratered object in the Solar System.
body: Callisto is almost as wide as Mercury and orbits Jupiter every 16.7 days. Its dark surface is crowded with craters.

Galileo's magnetometer detected a magnetic signal induced by Jupiter's changing field near Callisto, as at Europa. A salty ocean beneath the surface is the most likely explanation, but it is **Inferred**, and Europa's ocean is supported by more independent evidence.
ESA's Juice spacecraft, arriving at Jupiter in 2031, will study Callisto as one of three possibly ocean-bearing moons.
In the game, Callisto's map comes from NASA's 3D Resources and contains blank, filled-in areas where no usable images exist. Those patches, and all fine relief, are not real data.

entries.title: Saturn
entries.summary: The ringed giant: a hydrogen-helium planet less dense than water, circled by bright rings of ice that are only metres to tens of metres thick.
body: Saturn is the second-largest planet. Its average density, 0.69 g/cm³, is lower than that of water, and its fast 10.7-hour spin makes it the most flattened planet.
The main rings stretch from about 74,700 km to 136,800 km from Saturn's centre, yet they are only about 5 to 30 m thick. They are mostly water ice, polluted by 0.1 to 2% of darker, non-icy material.

How old are the rings? In its final orbits Cassini flew between the planet and the rings and weighed them, and its scientists concluded that the rings are much younger than Saturn. Cassini's dust measurements suggest an exposure age of no more than a few hundred million years. Later simulations argue that ring particles resist pollution, so the rings could be older than they look. The question is open.
Saturn has 274 confirmed moons on NASA's list, after 128 new discoveries were announced in March 2025. Titan and Enceladus are the most famous.
In the game, the globe and rings use Solar System Scope textures and the ring edges use NASA's measured radii. The globe's haze is **Generated**.

entries.title: Enceladus
entries.summary: A small, bright moon of Saturn that sprays jets of water ice from its south pole, fed by a global ocean beneath its shell.
body: Enceladus is only about 500 km across, yet it is geologically active today.

The Cassini spacecraft found warm fractures near its south pole venting jets of icy particles and water vapour. The jets supply material to Saturn's faint E ring and probably come from liquid water below the surface.
Over seven years Cassini tracked how Enceladus wobbles as it orbits. The wobble is too large for an icy shell frozen onto a rocky core, so the shell must float on a **global ocean**.

Flying through the plume, Cassini detected molecular hydrogen, a sign of water reacting with rock in hydrothermal processes, and later sodium phosphates, showing that the ocean holds phosphorus at concentrations at least 100 times higher than Earth's oceans. These are ingredients and energy sources that life as we know it uses; none of them is a detection of life.
In the game, Enceladus's map from NASA's 3D Resources is incomplete: large white regions are fill, not data. Fine relief is **Generated**.

entries.title: Titan
entries.summary: Saturn's largest moon: bigger than Mercury, wrapped in a thick nitrogen atmosphere, with rain, rivers and lakes of liquid methane and ethane.
body: Titan is the second-largest moon in the Solar System and the only moon with a substantial atmosphere. That atmosphere is mostly nitrogen with some methane, and its surface pressure is about 1.5 times Earth's.
At the surface it is 93.65 K (about -180 °C), so cold that methane and ethane can be liquid. Titan is the only place besides Earth known to have liquids on its surface.
The Huygens probe, released by the Cassini spacecraft, parachuted through the haze. Its pictures showed highlands cut by drainage channels and, after landing, ground that looks like a dry riverbed.
Cassini's radar later revealed more than 75 radar-dark patches near the north pole that are interpreted as lakes of liquid hydrocarbons.
NASA's Dragonfly rotorcraft is planned to launch no earlier than July 2028 to fly between sites on Titan.
In the game, Titan appears as an orange globe of haze. Its surface is hidden in visible light, and the game's haze and colours are a **Generated** approximation, not a surface map.

entries.title: Uranus
entries.summary: An ice giant tipped on its side, so that each pole spends decades in sunlight and then decades in darkness during its 84-year orbit.
body: Uranus's spin axis is tilted by about 98 degrees, so it appears to roll around the Sun on its side. Over its 84-year orbit each pole points almost straight at the Sun for part of the year.

It is an ice giant: models suggest that 80% or more of its mass is a hot, dense fluid of 'icy' materials such as water, methane and ammonia above a small rocky core. Methane in its atmosphere absorbs red light, which gives Uranus its blue-green colour.
William Herschel discovered Uranus on 13 March 1781. Its rings were found in 1977, when astronomers on the Kuiper Airborne Observatory watched a star blink several times as it passed behind them.
Voyager 2 flew past on 24 January 1986, returning detailed photos of the planet, its moons, its magnetic field and its dark rings.
In the game, Uranus uses a Solar System Scope map, and its haze is **Generated**.

entries.title: Neptune
entries.summary: The outermost planet: a cold, windy ice giant whose position was predicted by mathematics before astronomers identified it through a telescope.
body: Neptune orbits about 30 times farther from the Sun than Earth and takes almost 165 years to go around once.
It was the first planet located through mathematical prediction. Johann Galle found it on 23 September 1846, near the position predicted by Urbain Le Verrier and John Couch Adams.
Its winds are the fastest measured on any planet in the NASA fact sheets, up to about 580 m/s.
Voyager 2 flew past in August 1989. It saw a huge storm about the size of Earth, the Great Dark Spot, bright methane clouds, three main rings of very dark material and six new moons.
In the game, Neptune uses a Solar System Scope map, and its haze is **Generated**.

entries.title: Triton
entries.summary: Neptune's largest moon: a frozen world that orbits backwards and erupts plumes of dark material, probably a captured visitor from the Kuiper Belt.
body: Triton is the only large moon in the Solar System that orbits in the opposite direction to its planet's rotation. That backwards orbit is one reason scientists think it is a Kuiper Belt object captured by Neptune's gravity.
How it was captured is not known. One proposal is that Triton was once part of a pair of bodies, and a close pass by Neptune split the pair and kept Triton.
Voyager 2 found at least four active geyser-like plumes in 1989. Columns of dark material rose about 8 km and drifted more than 100 km downwind, even though the surface is only about 38 K.
Its surface is a rigid crust, probably water ice, coated with bright nitrogen frost and streaked by darker organic material.
Voyager 2 photographed only part of Triton during its brief flyby. In the game's map, areas without images are left blank; they are not real data, and fine relief is **Generated** everywhere.

entries.title: Pluto
entries.summary: A dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt with flowing glaciers, a water-ice crust and a hazy atmosphere, explored by New Horizons in 2015.
body: Clyde Tombaugh discovered Pluto on 18 February 1930. In 2006 the International Astronomical Union defined a planet more strictly, and Pluto became a dwarf planet because it has not cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit.
Pluto's orbit is tilted and elongated. It ranges from about 30 to 49 au from the Sun, so for part of each 248-year orbit Pluto is closer to the Sun than Neptune.

NASA's New Horizons flew past on 14 July 2015. It found surfaces of very different ages, a water-ice crust, convection in surface ice, wind streaks, glacial flow, and an extended atmosphere with a global haze layer and a surface pressure near 10 microbars.
Pluto and its large moon Charon always show each other the same face: they are mutually tidally locked.
In the game, Pluto's surface map is the USGS New Horizons mosaic. Areas New Horizons did not image have no data in the mosaic, and relief at small scales is **Generated**.

entries.title: Charon
entries.summary: Pluto's giant moon, half Pluto's width, locked face to face with it and marked by a reddish north pole and canyons deeper than the Grand Canyon.
body: Charon is about half the size of Pluto, the largest moon relative to its parent body that we know of. The pair is sometimes called a double dwarf planet.
Charon orbits every 6.39 days, exactly the time both Pluto and Charon take to rotate, so each always shows the other the same face.
New Horizons revealed tectonic features, including a trough at least 350 km long and up to 14 km deep, and a dark reddish cap at the north pole.

The red cap is thought to come from gas escaping Pluto that freezes onto Charon's cold winter pole and is changed by ultraviolet light into reddish compounds. This explanation is a model that fits the images; it is **Inferred**.
In the game, Charon's map is the USGS New Horizons mosaic. Areas without images have no data, and fine relief is **Generated**.

entries.title: TRAPPIST-1
entries.summary: An ultracool red dwarf about 40.7 light-years away, only a little larger than Jupiter, orbited by seven Earth-sized planets.
body: TRAPPIST-1 is an ultracool dwarf star of spectral type M8 V. It has about 9% of the Sun's mass and 12% of its radius, a surface temperature near 2,570 K, and about 1/1,800 of the Sun's luminosity. It is faint in visible light but relatively bright in the infrared.

In 2016 astronomers reported three Earth-sized planets transiting the star. A year later, an intensive campaign with NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope and ground-based telescopes revealed seven. The six inner planets form a near-resonant chain: their periods are close to ratios of small whole numbers, which suggests they formed farther out and migrated inward.

Because all seven planets transit, their sizes are measured. Because they tug on one another, their transit times shift slightly from orbit to orbit, and modelling those shifts gives masses precise to 3-5%. All seven have similar densities, consistent with rocky worlds somewhat poorer in iron than Earth, or Earth-like worlds with extra light material such as water.

The star is old, about 7.6 ± 2.2 billion years, and magnetically active. Starspots, bright faculae and flares contaminate JWST transit spectra of its planets, which is one reason their atmospheres are so hard to study.
In the game, every planet surface you see in this system is **Generated**: no telescope can image them.

entries.title: TRAPPIST-1 b
entries.summary: The innermost TRAPPIST-1 planet: Earth-sized, hot, and according to JWST most likely a dark bare rock without a thick atmosphere.
body: TRAPPIST-1 b circles its star in about 36 hours and receives roughly four times as much starlight as Earth gets from the Sun.
In 2023 JWST detected heat from its day side at 15 microns. The amount fits a planet with little or no atmosphere to carry heat around, and no sign of carbon dioxide.

Adding observations at 12.8 microns left two possibilities: an airless planet with a fresh, unweathered rocky surface, or a thick carbon-dioxide atmosphere with hazes. Broadband measurements alone could not decide.

JWST then followed the planet around its whole orbit. The day side glows at about 490 K, the night side shows no significant heat, and the hottest spot is not shifted. Atmospheres of 1 bar or more are strongly disfavoured: TRAPPIST-1 b is unlikely to have any substantial atmosphere.
**The surface you see in the game is Generated.** It is a plausible guess for a hot, airless rock, not an image.

entries.summary: An Earth-sized planet receiving a little more starlight than Venus does; JWST rules out a thick carbon-dioxide atmosphere like Venus's.
body: TRAPPIST-1 c orbits in 2.4 days and receives about twice the starlight Earth gets, a little more than Venus receives from the Sun.

JWST measured its day-side heat at 15 microns in 2023: a brightness temperature of 380 ± 31 K. That is too hot for a thick, carbon-dioxide-rich atmosphere, and a Venus-like atmosphere with sulfuric-acid clouds is disfavoured.

A later JWST phase curve found a day side near 369 K and a cold night side. TRAPPIST-1 c may be airless with a fairly reflective surface, or keep a thin, oxygen-rich atmosphere; atmospheres of 1 bar or more are strongly disfavoured.
If the planet formed with water, the lack of a thick atmosphere suggests it began relatively poor in volatiles.
**The surface you see in the game is Generated.** Its atmosphere, if any, is unknown.

entries.title: TRAPPIST-1 d
entries.summary: A small planet at the inner edge of TRAPPIST-1's habitable zone whose JWST spectrum is flat: no clear sign of an atmosphere.
body: TRAPPIST-1 d is about 79% of Earth's width and 39% of its mass, and receives about 1.1 times the starlight Earth does. That places it at the inner edge of the star's habitable zone.

JWST observed two transits with its near-infrared spectrograph. After correcting for the star's spots, which add slopes of 500-1,000 parts per million, the spectrum is flat to within about 100-150 ppm.

That rules out clear hydrogen-rich atmospheres and many heavier ones resembling a haze-free Titan, a cloud-free Venus, early Mars, or cloud-free versions of ancient and modern Earth. If d has an atmosphere, it is probably very thin or hidden by high-altitude haze or clouds.
**The surface you see in the game is Generated.** Whether TRAPPIST-1 d has any atmosphere is unknown.

entries.title: TRAPPIST-1 e
entries.summary: A habitable-zone planet that could keep liquid water on its surface if it has an atmosphere. Whether it has one is still unknown.
body: TRAPPIST-1 e is a little smaller than Earth and receives about two thirds of the starlight Earth gets. It lies in the star's habitable zone, where liquid water could exist on the surface if the planet has a suitable atmosphere.
JWST observed four transits in 2023. The spectra are strongly affected by the star's spots, which current star models cannot fully explain, so the team modelled that contamination statistically.

The data rule out cloudy, hydrogen-dominated atmospheres. They do not show strong evidence for or against any atmosphere: a bare rock fits, and so does a nitrogen-rich atmosphere with traces of carbon dioxide and methane. Carbon-dioxide-rich atmospheres as thick as Venus's are weakly disfavoured.
A longer JWST programme is now observing e right after transits of the airless planet b, to correct for the star's contamination more directly.
**Any oceans, clouds, ice or land you see on this planet in the game are Generated.** Its atmosphere and surface are unknown.

body: TRAPPIST-1 f is almost exactly Earth's size and mass and receives about 37% of the starlight Earth gets, in the cooler part of the habitable zone.

The first JWST transit spectra of f, from five transits, were published in September 2026. Every visit included at least one stellar flare, but unlike for the inner planets, the team saw no sign of contamination from unseen starspots.

The cleanest visits rule out hydrogen- and helium-rich atmospheres with surface pressures above about 20 millibars. Limits on heavier atmospheres depend on how the data are processed, so whether f has an atmosphere remains open.
**The surface you see in the game is Generated.** Its atmosphere is unknown.

entries.title: TRAPPIST-1 g
entries.summary: The largest TRAPPIST-1 planet, slightly bigger than Earth, in the outer part of the habitable zone; very little is known about its atmosphere.
body: TRAPPIST-1 g is about 13% wider and 32% more massive than Earth, the largest planet in the system, and receives about a quarter of the starlight Earth gets.
It counts as one of the system's habitable-zone planets, together with e and f. Its equilibrium temperature of about 200 K means it would be frozen unless an atmosphere keeps it warmer.

Earlier transit spectra taken from space and from the ground ruled out cloud-free, hydrogen-rich atmospheres for every TRAPPIST-1 planet, including g. JWST has observed all seven planets, but this Codex's sources contain no published JWST measurement of g's atmosphere as of October 2026.
**The surface you see in the game is Generated.** Its atmosphere is unknown.

entries.title: TRAPPIST-1 h
entries.summary: The outermost known TRAPPIST-1 planet: small, cold, and receiving about one seventh of the starlight Earth gets.
body: TRAPPIST-1 h is about three quarters of Earth's width and a third of its mass, and orbits every 18.8 days.

It receives about 14% of the starlight Earth gets, so without a thick greenhouse atmosphere it would be frozen. Like its siblings, it cannot have a cloud-free, hydrogen-rich atmosphere; beyond that, nothing is known about its air.

JWST transit timings show that h's transits have drifted by up to tens of minutes from the 2021 forecast, a reminder that even 'measured' orbits are models that get updated. That result comes from a research note that, as far as we know, has not been peer reviewed.
**The surface you see in the game is Generated.** Its atmosphere is unknown.

entries.title: Sirius
entries.summary: The brightest star in the night sky: a hot white star 8.6 light-years away with a faint companion, Sirius B, the nearest known white dwarf.
body: Sirius A is a hot, metallic-line A-type star about twice the Sun's mass. Seen from Earth it is the brightest star in the night sky, because it is both luminous and close.

It has a companion, **Sirius B**, a white dwarf: the dense core left behind by a star that has already finished its life. Sirius B has about the Sun's mass, and it is the brightest and nearest white dwarf known.
The two stars orbit each other every 50.13 years. Combining nearly two decades of Hubble images with historical measurements back to the 19th century gives their masses to about 1%.

The system is young, roughly 230 million years old. Sirius B's progenitor must have been more massive than Sirius A to have evolved first, and how the two interacted while keeping such an eccentric orbit is still a puzzle.
In the game, Sirius's position and brightness come from the HYG catalogue, based on Hipparcos measurements.

entries.title: Alpha Centauri A (Rigil Kentaurus)
entries.summary: The nearest Sun-like star: a yellow G-type star a little larger and more massive than the Sun, paired with Alpha Centauri B about 4.37 light-years away.
body: Alpha Centauri A and B form a binary that orbits every 80 years or so. Together with the faint red dwarf Proxima Centauri they make up the closest star system to the Sun.
A is a G2 V star like the Sun but about 22% wider and about 13% more massive. Its radius was measured directly by combining its angular size, from optical interferometry, with its distance.

In 2024 JWST imaged a faint point of light, called S1, about 2 au from A in the star's habitable zone. If real, it would be a cold giant planet. It was not seen again in 2025, so it remains an **unconfirmed candidate**.
The pair moves 3.7 arcseconds per year across the sky. In May 2028 A will pass extremely close to a distant background star, a rare chance to probe the system with gravitational lensing.
In the game, A and B are placed using the HYG catalogue's Hipparcos distance (4.32 ly); later measurements put the pair about 1% farther away.

entries.title: Alpha Centauri B (Toliman)
entries.summary: The smaller partner of Alpha Centauri A: an orange K-type star a little less massive than the Sun.
body: Alpha Centauri B is a K1 V star, cooler and smaller than the Sun, with about 86% of its radius and 97% of its mass. Its proper name, recognized by the IAU, is Toliman.
B and A orbit each other every 80 years or so, and the pair is circled at a great distance by Proxima Centauri.

An Earth-mass planet candidate, 'Alpha Centauri Bb', was once announced from tiny radial-velocity wobbles of B. A re-analysis showed that its 3.24-day signal almost certainly came from the way the observations were spaced in time, not from a planet. No planet is confirmed around B.
In the game, B is placed using the HYG catalogue's Hipparcos distance, the same as A.

entries.title: Proxima Centauri
entries.summary: The closest star to the Sun: a small, flaring red dwarf 4.25 light-years away with at least two planets, including Earth-mass Proxima b.
body: Proxima Centauri is a red dwarf with about 12% of the Sun's mass, 14% of its radius and a surface near 3,050 K. It gives out only about 0.1% of the Sun's light, so although it is our nearest star it is far too faint to see without a telescope.

Gaia measured its parallax to better than 0.01%, putting it 4.2465 light-years away. Proxima is gravitationally bound to Alpha Centauri A and B, circling them roughly every 550,000 years; today it is near the far point of that orbit, about 13,000 au from the pair.

Two planets are confirmed by the radial-velocity method. **Proxima b** (2016) has at least 1.06 Earth masses and orbits every 11.2 days in the star's habitable zone. **Proxima d**, confirmed in 2025, has at least 0.26 Earth masses and orbits every 5.1 days. A third signal, a candidate called Proxima c with a period of about 5 years, is not confirmed.

Proxima is an active flare star. In March 2016 a superflare made it about 68 times brighter in visible light, briefly reaching naked-eye brightness. Repeated flares like this could strip the ozone from an Earth-like atmosphere on Proxima b, so its habitability is very uncertain.
In the game, Proxima is placed using the HYG catalogue's Hipparcos parallax (4.23 ly), about 0.5% closer than Gaia's value.

entries.title: Proxima Centauri b
entries.summary: An Earth-mass planet in the habitable zone of the nearest star. We know its minimum mass and orbit, but not its size, atmosphere or surface.
body: Proxima b was announced in 2016 after astronomers measured Proxima Centauri wobbling towards and away from us every 11.2 days. Later observations with the ESPRESSO and NIRPS spectrographs confirmed it.
The radial-velocity method gives only a **minimum mass**, at least 1.06 Earth masses, because we do not know how the orbit is tilted to our line of sight.

It orbits about 0.05 au from its star, about one twentieth of Earth's distance from the Sun, and lies in Proxima's habitable zone. It may be tidally locked, as many close-in exoplanets are thought to be, but that has not been measured.
Its radius, whether it has an atmosphere, and what its surface is like are all unknown. Proxima's strong flares are a serious challenge for any atmosphere or life.
**Anything shown for Proxima b's surface in the game is Generated.**

entries.title: Barnard's Star
entries.summary: A faint, old red dwarf 6 light-years away that races across our sky faster than any star known in 1916, and hosts four tiny planets.
body: Barnard's Star is the second-closest stellar system to the Sun after Alpha Centauri. It is a single, old red dwarf, too faint to see without a telescope.

In 1916 E. E. Barnard found that it moves about 10.3 arcseconds per year across the sky, the largest proper motion then known. Gaia measures 10.39 arcseconds per year, and its spectrum shows it approaching us at about 110 km/s.

Barnard's Star has a long history of claimed planets that did not survive scrutiny. A super-Earth candidate announced in 2018 turned out to be an alias of the star's 145-day rotation signal, not a planet.

In 2024 and 2025, extremely precise radial-velocity measurements with the ESPRESSO and MAROON-X spectrographs found four planets, now confirmed, each with at least about 0.2 to 0.3 Earth masses and orbits of 2.3 to 6.7 days, all closer to the star than its habitable zone. The data rule out planets heavier than about 0.57 Earth masses in the habitable zone.
In the game, Barnard's Star is placed using the HYG catalogue's Hipparcos distance, which agrees with Gaia to about 0.2%.

entries.title: Betelgeuse
entries.summary: A red supergiant in Orion hundreds of times wider than the Sun, famous for its Great Dimming in 2019-2020 and expected to end its life as a supernova.
body: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant: a massive star late in its life, swollen to roughly 750 times the Sun's radius according to models. Red supergiants are the most common final stage in the lives of stars born with about 8 to 35 solar masses; the stage lasts roughly 100,000 years and ends in a supernova. Nobody can predict when Betelgeuse will explode.

Its distance is uncertain. Hipparcos gives about 500 light-years with a large error; a model-based study gives about 550; other measurements quoted by astronomers suggest about 720. So the light you see left the star roughly 500 to 700 years ago.

Between November 2019 and March 2020 Betelgeuse faded to magnitude 1.6, far below its usual range. Images showed its southern half ten times darker than usual. The best explanation is a cloud of dust that formed after a cool patch appeared on the star's surface, following an outflow of material seen in ultraviolet light.

Betelgeuse may have a small companion star on a roughly 6-year orbit. A 2024 image from the Gemini North telescope shows a probable detection, but only at about 1.5 sigma, and Hubble did not detect it in ultraviolet light. It is not confirmed.
In the game, Betelgeuse is placed using the HYG catalogue's Hipparcos distance. The size the game computes for it from magnitude and colour is much smaller than detailed models suggest.

entries.title: Polaris
entries.summary: The North Star: a pulsating supergiant less than a degree from the north celestial pole, with a faint companion that reveals its mass.
body: Polaris lies within about 0.74 degrees of the north celestial pole (at the J2000 epoch), so as Earth turns, it barely moves in the sky while the other stars circle around it.

It is a Cepheid variable, a yellow supergiant that pulsates. It also has unusual habits: its pulsation period changes quickly, its brightness variations have changed in size, and it once jumped in phase.

A faint companion orbits Polaris every 30 years on an elongated orbit. Following it with the CHARA interferometer gave Polaris a mass of 5.13 ± 0.28 solar masses. At its measured distance, Polaris is brighter than models predict for that mass.
The same observations hint at spots on its surface, which could explain a 120-day brightness cycle as the star's rotation. This is suggestive, not yet confirmed.
In the game, Polaris is placed using the HYG catalogue's Hipparcos distance of about 433 light-years.

entries.title: Vega
entries.summary: A bright white star 25 light-years away that spins so fast it bulges at the equator, seen almost pole-on, and surrounded by a wide disc of dust.
body: Vega has long served as a standard star: astronomers used it to calibrate both stellar spectra and brightness measurements.

Interferometers revealed that Vega rotates at more than 90% of the speed at which it would start to fly apart, and that we happen to look almost straight down on its pole. Its poles are about 2,250 K hotter than its equator, which explains why it looked oddly bright for its type.

In 1984 the IRAS satellite found that Vega gives off far more infrared light than a star of its temperature should: the first such excess seen around a normal main-sequence star. It comes from solid particles orbiting the star, thought to be material left over from its formation.

JWST images show the disc to be remarkably smooth and symmetric, with a broad outer belt from about 80 to 170 au. That argues against Saturn-mass planets beyond about 10 au, though a smaller planet could still be hiding closer in.
In the game, Vega is placed using the HYG catalogue's Hipparcos distance.

entries.title: Measured, Inferred, Generated
entries.summary: Every object and number in Known Sky carries a badge saying how we know it: Measured, Inferred or Generated.
body: **Measured** means the value comes from observations, as published by a space mission, a catalogue or a peer-reviewed paper: Earth's radius, the Moon's elevation map, the size of TRAPPIST-1 e. Measured values still have uncertainties, and the Codex shows them when they are known.

**Inferred** means the value is not observed directly but follows from measurements through physics, models or calculation: a planet's density from its mass and radius, a star's age, an equilibrium temperature, or a distance in light-years computed from a parallax. Inferred values are only as good as the models behind them.

**Generated** means the game made it up within physical rules because no data exist: the rocks and small craters under your ship, the terrain of an exoplanet, the glow of a star's surface. Generation is seeded, so every player sees the same world, but it is not real.

The Codex never presents Inferred or Generated content as fact. When better data arrive, such as a new Gaia release or a new JWST spectrum, an object can be promoted from Generated to Inferred or Measured.

Measured does not mean final. When JWST timed new transits of TRAPPIST-1 h, they had drifted by up to tens of minutes from the 2021 forecast. Science keeps updating its numbers, and so does this Codex.

entries.title: Stellar parallax
entries.summary: As Earth circles the Sun, nearby stars shift slightly against more distant ones. Measuring that shift gives the most direct distances to the stars.
body: Hold a finger at arm's length and close each eye in turn: the finger jumps against the background. Nearby stars do the same as Earth moves around its orbit. The size of the shift, the parallax angle, together with the size of Earth's orbit gives the distance by simple trigonometry.
The shifts are tiny. Even for the nearest stars they are less than one arcsecond, about the apparent width of a small coin seen from four kilometres away.
The first stellar parallaxes were measured in the late 1830s, by Friedrich Bessel, Wilhelm Struve and Thomas Henderson.
A star with a parallax of one arcsecond is one **parsec** away, about 3.26 light-years. Proxima Centauri's parallax of 0.768 arcseconds puts it 1.302 parsecs, or 4.25 light-years, away.

ESA's Hipparcos satellite (1989-1993) measured parallaxes for 118,218 stars. Gaia's third data release has parallaxes for about 1.46 billion sources, and its fourth release is scheduled for 2 December 2026.

entries.title: The transit method
entries.summary: When a planet passes in front of its star, the starlight dips slightly. Repeating dips reveal the planet's size and orbit; most known exoplanets were found this way.
body: If a planet's orbit is lined up almost edge-on with our view, the planet crosses the face of its star once per orbit and blocks a little of its light. The fraction blocked is roughly the planet's disc area divided by the star's.
Earth crossing the Sun would dim it by less than 0.01%. TRAPPIST-1 e, crossing a star only 12% as wide as the Sun, dims it by about 0.5%. Small stars make small planets easier to find.
The first exoplanet seen to transit its star, HD 209458 b, was reported in 2000. Its dimming showed a gas giant about 1.3 times Jupiter's radius.

NASA's Kepler mission monitored more than 150,000 stars at once, and NASA's TESS mission has continued the search. Of the 6,445 confirmed planets in the NASA Exoplanet Archive on 11 October 2026, 4,781 were discovered by transits.
A transit gives a planet's size, not its mass. Masses come from radial velocities or, in tightly packed systems like TRAPPIST-1, from transit-timing variations.

entries.title: Transit-timing variations
entries.summary: In a system with several planets, each tugs on the others, so transits arrive a little early or late. Those timing shifts can weigh the planets.
body: A lone planet on an unchanging orbit transits like clockwork. Add another planet and their gravity nudges each other, so transits come early or late, typically by minutes and sometimes much more.
In 2005 two groups showed that these timing variations could reveal unseen planets, even ones with about Earth's mass, especially when the planets are near an orbital resonance.
Kepler-9 (2010) was confirmed this way: two Saturn-size planets whose orbital periods were changing by 4 and 39 minutes per orbit, a sign of mutual gravity near a 2:1 resonance.

The seven TRAPPIST-1 planets are packed so tightly that their transit times pin down all seven masses to 3-5%. That is equivalent to measuring the star's wobble to 2.5 cm/s, about a hundred times finer than current radial-velocity instruments can.
Timing models have to be updated as new data arrive: new JWST timings show TRAPPIST-1 h drifting by up to tens of minutes from the 2021 forecast.

entries.title: The radial-velocity method
entries.summary: A planet and its star orbit their common centre of mass, so the star wobbles towards and away from us. Tiny Doppler shifts in its light reveal the planet.
body: When a star moves towards us its light is shifted very slightly to the blue; when it moves away, to the red. Precise spectrographs turn these Doppler shifts into a speed along our line of sight, the radial velocity.

In 1995 Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz used periodic changes in the radial velocity of the Sun-like star 51 Pegasi to find a Jupiter-mass companion only about 8 million km from its star, well inside the distance at which Mercury orbits the Sun.
The best instruments now detect wobbles well under one metre per second, slower than a walking pace: Barnard's Star b moves its star by only 55 ± 7 cm/s.

The method gives a **minimum mass**, because an orbit tilted to our line of sight hides part of the motion. Stellar activity and the timing of the observations can also mimic planets: claimed planets around Alpha Centauri B and Barnard's Star turned out to be false alarms.
Of the 6,445 confirmed planets in the NASA Exoplanet Archive on 11 October 2026, 1,203 were discovered by radial velocity, including Proxima b and d.

entries.title: Light-travel time and lookback
entries.summary: Light is fast but not infinitely fast. Whatever you look at, you see as it was when its light set out.
body: Light in a vacuum travels at 299,792,458 metres per second. Sunlight takes 499 seconds, about 8 minutes 19 seconds, to reach Earth, and moonlight about 1.3 seconds. A radio signal from Neptune takes about four hours.

A light-year is the distance light travels in one Julian year, about 9.46 trillion km. The light you see from Proxima Centauri left it 4.25 years ago, from TRAPPIST-1 about 40.7 years ago, and from Betelgeuse somewhere around 500 to 700 years ago.

So the night sky mixes many moments of the past. The farthest stars in this game's catalogue are about 3,200 light-years away: you see them as they were around 3,200 years ago. Some of them may have changed since.
The game's HUD shows real distances and light-travel times. Only the speed at which your ship crosses them is fiction.

entries.title: Why the sky is blue
entries.summary: Air molecules scatter blue light much more strongly than red light, so the daytime sky glows blue and the setting Sun looks red.
body: Sunlight contains all colours. On its way through the atmosphere some of it is scattered in all directions by gas molecules, which are far smaller than the wavelength of light. For such small scatterers the scattering rises steeply at shorter wavelengths, as one over the wavelength to the fourth power. This is **Rayleigh scattering**.
Blue light at 440 nm is therefore scattered about 5.7 times more strongly than red light at 680 nm. Look away from the Sun and you see that scattered blue light.
When the Sun is low, its light crosses much more air. Most of the blue is scattered out of the direct beam, leaving the reds and yellows; dust and other small particles can make sunsets redder still.
Other skies differ. On Mars, fine dust lets blue light through near the direction of the Sun, so rovers have photographed bluish sunsets under an orange daytime sky.

The game computes Earth's sky with a published model of Rayleigh and Mie scattering (Bruneton & Neyret 2008) using scattering coefficients for real air, so the colours are **Inferred**, not painted. The hazes of Mars, Venus, Titan and the giant planets are simpler **Generated** approximations.

entries.title: Tidal locking
entries.summary: Tides gradually force a moon or planet to spin once per orbit, so it keeps the same face towards its partner. Our Moon is the classic example.
body: A moon is stretched slightly by its planet's gravity. If it spins faster or slower than it orbits, that bulge is dragged around, flexing the interior and turning energy into heat, until the spin matches the orbit.

The Moon rotates once every 27.3 days, the same time it takes to orbit Earth, so its far side always faces away. All the large moons in the Solar System are tidally locked to their planets, including the four Galilean moons, Titan and Triton.
Pluto and Charon go one step further: each is locked to the other, so both always show the same face, and a day on either lasts 6.39 Earth days.
The tides that locked the Moon are still at work, pushing it outward by about 3.8 cm per year and slowly lengthening Earth's day.

Planets very close to small stars, such as the TRAPPIST-1 planets or Proxima b, are expected to be tidally locked too, with permanent day and night sides. That is a strong expectation, not a measurement. JWST's view of TRAPPIST-1 b, with a hot day side and no detectable night-side heat, is consistent with it.

entries.title: The habitable zone
entries.summary: The range of distances from a star where a rocky planet with the right atmosphere could keep liquid water on its surface. Being in it does not make a planet habitable.
body: Every star has a habitable zone: too close and water boils away, too far and it freezes. Hotter, brighter stars have wider zones farther out; dim red dwarfs have narrow zones very close in.
The edges come from climate models. A widely used 2013 calculation puts the conservative habitable zone of our Sun between about 0.99 and 1.70 au, which places Earth near the inner edge.

Astronomers compare the starlight a planet receives with what Earth receives rather than its temperature, because the real temperature depends on unknowns such as clouds, reflectivity and greenhouse gases.

Being in the zone is not enough. Mars lies inside the Sun's conservative habitable zone, yet it is a cold desert today. Planets of red dwarfs also face strong flares: superflares from Proxima Centauri could strip the ozone from an Earth-like atmosphere.
In this game, TRAPPIST-1 e, f and g lie in their star's habitable zone (d at its inner edge), and so does Proxima b. Whether any of them has an atmosphere, let alone water, is unknown.

entries.title: How JPL knows where the planets are
entries.summary: JPL's ephemerides are numerical models of the Solar System, fitted to decades of radar, laser and spacecraft measurements. The game reads planet and moon positions from them.
body: An ephemeris tells you where a body is at any moment. JPL builds its planetary ephemerides by numerically integrating the orbits of the Sun, planets and Moon and adjusting the model until it matches the observations.

Those observations include radio ranging and very-long-baseline interferometry of spacecraft such as Juno at Jupiter and Cassini at Saturn, lunar laser ranging, and stellar occultations by Pluto measured against the Gaia star catalogue.

DE440, released in 2021, covers the years 1550 to 2650. Its sibling DE441 leaves out a friction term between the Moon's core and mantle so that it can run from the year -13,200 to +17,191, at slightly lower accuracy for the present century.
Moons have their own JPL satellite ephemerides, fitted to spacecraft and telescope data. JPL's Horizons service combines all of these.

The game downloaded Horizons positions for 2026 to 2032 and stored them as compact polynomials. Checked against separate Horizons samples, the fit stays within about 7 m for the Moon and about 1.5 km at worst (Uranus), far smaller than anything you could notice.

entries.title: Gaia, Hipparcos and the HYG catalogue
entries.summary: The stars you can fly to come from the HYG catalogue, built mainly on ESA's Hipparcos mission. ESA's Gaia has since measured vastly more stars far more precisely.
body: ESA's Hipparcos satellite operated from 1989 to 1993 and measured the positions, distances and motions of 118,218 stars. A 2007 re-reduction of its data improved the accuracy for most bright stars by up to a factor of four.

The HYG database combines Hipparcos with the Yale Bright Star Catalogue and the Gliese Catalogue of Nearby Stars, adding names and designations. Known Sky uses HYG version 4.1 (CC BY-SA 4.0): 109,400 stars within about 990 parsecs, roughly 3,200 light-years.

Gaia launched on 19 December 2013 and scanned the whole sky again and again from near the Sun-Earth L2 point. Its third data release (2022) gives positions, parallaxes and motions for about 1.46 billion sources. Gaia DR4, due on 2 December 2026, will cover more than two billion stars and other objects.

The game uses Gaia in two places: precise distances quoted in this Codex for some nearby stars, and the glowing Milky Way backdrop, an ESA image of the light of 1.8 billion stars from Gaia EDR3. The stars themselves still use Hipparcos-era distances, which for distant stars can be quite uncertain: Betelgeuse's Hipparcos parallax has an error of about 13%.

entries.title: The drive is fiction
entries.summary: Known Sky's universe is real, but its interstellar drive is not. Nothing with mass can reach the speed of light, and warp drives and wormholes remain speculative mathematics.
body: Special relativity, published by Albert Einstein in 1905, makes the speed of light, 299,792,458 m/s, a limit: an object with mass would need unlimited energy to reach it.
NASA's Voyager 1, the most distant human-made object, travels at about 17 km/s relative to the Sun. At that speed, crossing the distance to Proxima Centauri would take about 75,000 years.

In the game, an interstellar jump takes roughly half a minute whatever the distance. Crossing 4.25 light-years in about 25 seconds would mean moving about five million times faster than light. That is pure fiction, and it is labelled **Generated**.

General relativity does allow some exotic solutions on paper. In 1994 Miguel Alcubierre described a 'warp drive' that contracts space ahead of a ship and expands it behind, so the ship could outpace light as seen from outside. It needs 'exotic matter' with negative energy density, and later calculations found the total energy required to be physically unattainable.

Traversable wormholes, shortcuts through spacetime, were described by Morris and Thorne in 1988 as a teaching tool. They need material whose tension exceeds its energy density; no known material behaves that way, though the authors noted it could not be ruled out firmly. There is no known way to build a warp drive or a wormhole.

entries.title: What the game's surfaces are
entries.summary: Some surfaces in Known Sky are spacecraft maps, some are artist-processed maps, and all fine detail is generated. Here is which is which.

**Moon:** colour from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera mosaic, processed for natural colour by NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio, with the polar regions filled from laser-altimeter brightness; elevation from LOLA at about 3.8 km spacing. Smaller craters are Generated.
**Pluto and Charon:** New Horizons global mosaics published by the USGS. Regions the spacecraft did not image have no data.

**Other moons** (Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto, Enceladus, Titan, Phobos, Deimos, Triton): spacecraft-based maps from NASA's 3D Resources. Some contain blank fill where no images exist, and Titan's shows haze, not ground. Their relief is Generated.

**Planets** (Mercury, Venus's clouds, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn and its rings, Uranus, Neptune): Solar System Scope textures. Their makers say they are based on NASA imagery, colour-tuned, slightly over-saturated, and that unmapped gaps are filled with invented terrain. Real laser-altimeter topography exists for Mars but the game does not use it yet; relief on rocky planets is Generated, and giant-planet clouds are fixed snapshots.

entries.title: Star brightness in the game
entries.summary: Stars keep their real brightness relative to each other, computed from catalogue magnitudes and distances, but the overall brightness is turned up so you can see them.
body: Astronomers measure brightness in magnitudes, a backwards logarithmic scale: a difference of 5 magnitudes is a factor of 100 in brightness, and smaller numbers are brighter. Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, is magnitude -1.44; the Sun seen from Earth is -26.74.

The game takes each star's absolute magnitude from the HYG catalogue and its distance from your ship, and recomputes its apparent brightness every frame. Fly towards a star and it brightens according to the inverse-square law; brightness ratios between stars are preserved.

The overall level is an artistic choice. Your eyes adapt to the dark far more than a camera exposed for sunlit planets, so the game turns up all stars and the Milky Way together and draws stars down to about magnitude 7.5. That exaggeration is **Generated**.
Star colours come from each star's catalogue colour index, converted to a temperature with a black-body formula, so they are **Inferred**.

When you travel to a star, the game also estimates its size from its visual magnitude and colour with a simple formula. This works reasonably for Sun-like stars but makes very red stars far too small, because the formula counts only visible light: for Proxima Centauri it gives about 0.02 solar radii, against a measured 0.14. Detailed models make Betelgeuse about three times larger than the game's estimate.
